raw_response:
I am seventy years old. I have farmed this land in Quzhou since I was a boy, and my father farmed it before me. I only finished primary school, but I know this soil and this weather better than any book. At my age, I do not have the strength or the heart to gamble on new crops. I will plant what has always fed my family: winter wheat on my ten mu, and follow it with summer maize on the same ten mu. That is the double-cropping rotation every household around here trusts.

For wheat, I will rotary-till the field before sowing, because that breaks up the stubble and makes a good seedbed. I will sow an improved variety—maybe Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502—using seed I bought from the cooperative. I will put down a basal compound fertilizer and then topdress with nitrogen. Over the season I will irrigate three times: once when the wheat greens up, once at jointing, and once at filling. I will spray pesticides three or four times to keep aphids, rust, and weeds under control.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will plant maize right away. I see no need to till again; I will plant no-till into the wheat stubble to save labor and fuel. I will use a hybrid maize such as Denghai 605, because the yield is steady and the grain buyers know it. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat, and I will irrigate it twice—at sowing and at the big-trumpet stage. Three rounds of pesticides will be enough for the maize.

This plan is not fancy, but it is safe. At my age, safe is what matters.
